cases.query: What is ECG and when was it established?
cases.reference_answer: ECG (Electricity Company of Ghana) is a limited liability company wholly owned by the Government of Ghana. Ghana's first government-sponsored public electricity supply began in 1914, and ECG remains the primary electricity distributor across southern Ghana, serving residential, commercial, and industrial customers. Its mission is to provide quality, reliable, and safe electricity services to support Ghana's economic growth, guided by the ENERGY core values: Excellence, Nurturing, Ethical, Reliability, Growth, and You.
cases.candidate_answer: ECG stands for Electricity Company of Ghana. However, the provided knowledge base does not specify when ECG was established. For more information, you can contact ECG's general support at 0302 611 611.

cases.query: Which districts are part of the Tema region?
cases.reference_answer: The Tema Region covers districts including Ada, Afienya, Ashaiman, Juapong, Krobo, Nungua, Prampram, Tema North, and Tema South.
cases.candidate_answer: The Tema Region districts include: Ada, Afienya, Ashaiman, Juapong, Krobo, Nungua, Prampram, Tema North, and Tema South.

cases.query: Why do I still have to pay a charge on my bill even though I don't use much electricity?
cases.reference_answer: In addition to charges for the electricity you actually consume, ECG bills include a fixed monthly service charge that covers maintenance of the network equipment serving your connection. This service charge applies every month regardless of how much power you use, and it continues to accrue even if your meter has been disconnected, since your account remains active in ECG's database.
cases.candidate_answer: The charge you're referring to is likely the service charge. According to our billing information, this is a monthly charge for customer services rendered, covering maintenance of the network equipment, and it continues even when a meter is disconnected. If you're a low-consumption household, you might be eligible for the Lifeline band, which has a lower service charge. You can check the PURC website or visit an ECG office for more information on residential tariffs.

cases.query: My prepaid meter card got lost, what should I do?
cases.reference_answer: If your prepaid card is missing, report it at your ECG District Office along with a copy of your vending receipt. ECG will issue you a new programmed card, and a replacement fee applies.
cases.candidate_answer: To replace a lost prepaid meter card, register at your District Office with a copy of your vending receipt. They will issue a new programmed card for a replacement fee. Contact your District Office for more information and assistance.

cases.query: What documents do I need to apply for a new low voltage electricity connection?
cases.reference_answer: For a new low voltage connection, submit a completed service form with a GHC 10 registration fee, together with an Installation Completion Certificate signed by a licensed electrician, a valid ID (National ID, Passport, Voter's ID, or Driver's License), and the original plus a photocopy of your site plan. Businesses must also provide proof of business operation. After an ECG inspection and payment of the cost estimate, connection is completed within 3 working days if lines already exist, or up to 5 days for extensions of up to 2 poles.
cases.candidate_answer: To apply for a new low voltage electricity connection, you'll need to submit a completed service form, site plan, and ID. Additionally, you'll need an Installation Completion Certificate signed by a licensed electrician, and proof of identification such as a National ID, Passport, Voters ID, or Drivers License. Businesses must also provide proof of business operation.

cases.query: How do I get my power reconnected after it was disconnected for non-payment?
cases.reference_answer: To get reconnected, settle all outstanding bills and pay the approved reconnection fee at your ECG District Office. Your meter will then be reconnected by ECG's reconnection team, usually the same day, once a team is available.
cases.candidate_answer: To reconnect after disconnection, settle all outstanding bills and pay the approved reconnection fee at your District Office. Your meter will be reconnected as soon as the reconnection team is available, usually within the same day. Please contact your District Office for more information.

cases.query: What counts as an illegal electricity connection?
cases.reference_answer: An illegal connection is obtaining electricity from an unauthorized source, which includes direct connections without a meter, unapproved meter transfers, meter tampering or bypass, unauthorized network extensions, unauthorized redistribution of supply, or reconnecting your own supply after a legal disconnection. Only qualified, authorized ECG personnel may reconnect a meter, and there is a cash reward for reporting confirmed power theft to 0302 611 611.
cases.candidate_answer: An illegal connection is the acquisition of electricity services from an unauthorized person or source. Examples include: direct connections without meters, meter transfers without approval, meter tampering, meter bypass, unauthorized network extensions, or self-reconnection after legal disconnection.

cases.query: What should I do if I see a fallen or sagging power line?
cases.reference_answer: Stay well away from a sagging or fallen power line. Do not touch the wire or anything it is in contact with, such as metal fences or standing water, and do not attempt to move it, since even a fallen tree touching a line can conduct high voltage. Call ECG immediately on 0302 611 611, or the emergency line 0800-POWER (0800-76937), and do not approach the area.
cases.candidate_answer: If you see a fallen or sagging power line, stay away at a distance. Do not touch the wire or contact objects it touches. Call ECG immediately on 0302 611 611.

cases.query: How do I report a fault to ECG?
cases.reference_answer: You can report a fault by contacting your ECG District Office, calling 0302 611 611 or 0551 444 011, or using the online portal at cx.eservicesafrica.com. Emergency faults are prioritized, and unresolved complaints can be escalated to PURC at purc.com.gh.
cases.candidate_answer: To report a fault, you can contact your District Office, call 0302 611 611 or 0551 444 011, or use the online portal at cx.eservicesafrica.com.

cases.query: What usually causes unplanned power outages in Ghana?
cases.reference_answer: Unplanned outages are commonly caused by broken high-tension poles from vehicle accidents or weather, faults on 11kV or 33kV feeder lines, transformer overloads or failures, underground or overhead cable faults, fire outbreaks near equipment, and upstream challenges from GRIDCo or VRA. Restoration time depends on the fault type: broken poles may take several hours to fix, while transformer faults can take a day or more.
cases.candidate_answer: Unplanned power outages in Ghana are commonly caused by factors such as broken high-tension poles, feeder faults, transformer overloads or failures, cable faults, and fire outbreaks near equipment.

cases.query: How can I apply to get street lighting installed in my area?
cases.reference_answer: To install street lighting, apply through your local Assembly or ECG District Manager with a layout of the area. ECG invites estimates from certified contractors, the General Manager verifies transformer capacity, the applicant pays a deposit, and ECG then authorizes a contractor to proceed. The contractor is paid from the deposited amount once the work is completed.
cases.candidate_answer: To apply for street lighting installation, submit an application through your Assembly or District Manager with an area layout. ECG will then invite estimates from certified contractors, verify transformer capacity, and authorize a contractor to proceed after you pay a deposit. For more information, contact ECG at 0302 611 611.

cases.query: What is PURC and how is it different from ECG?
cases.reference_answer: PURC (the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission) is the independent government regulator of electricity and water utilities in Ghana, established in October 1997 under Act 538. PURC is not ECG. It is the body that sets and approves the tariffs ECG is allowed to charge, monitors service standards, and handles complaints when a utility does not resolve a customer's issue, including billing disputes escalated from ECG's District level.
cases.candidate_answer: PURC (Public Utilities Regulatory Commission) is an independent regulator of electricity and water utility services in Ghana. It sets guidelines for utility rates, examines and approves tariffs, and protects consumer interests. ECG (Electricity Company of Ghana) is a utility company that provides electricity services. PURC is not ECG, but rather the independent body that oversees and regulates ECG's activities, including setting and approving the rates ECG can charge. For complaints or issues not resolved by ECG, customers can escalate to PURC.

cases.query: What is the current electricity tariff for a residential customer using 200 units a month?
cases.reference_answer: For a residential customer using 200 kWh a month, that usage falls in the 0-300 kWh band, billed at 203.7509 GHp/kWh, plus the standard residential service charge, effective 1st July 2026. Customers in the Lifeline band (0-30 kWh) pay a lower rate of 89.9315 GHp/kWh with a reduced Lifeline service charge. Since PURC revises tariffs roughly every quarter, confirm the current rate via the ECG PowerApp or purc.com.gh.

cases.query: What is the Lifeline electricity tariff band and who does it apply to?
cases.reference_answer: The Lifeline band covers residential customers using 0-30 kWh per month and exists to keep electricity affordable for the smallest consumers. As of 1st July 2026, it is billed at 89.9315 GHp/kWh with a lower Lifeline service charge of 213.0000 GHp/month, separate from the standard residential service charge.

cases.query: What tariff applies to a small business or shop?
cases.reference_answer: Non-residential customers such as shops and small offices are billed 183.9549 GHp/kWh for the first 300 kWh per month and 224.0395 GHp/kWh for usage above 301 kWh, plus a non-residential service charge of 1242.8245 GHp/month, effective 1st July 2026. Larger businesses with higher power demand are instead billed under the Special Load Tariff.

cases.query: How are large industrial customers billed for electricity?
cases.reference_answer: Large industrial or high-demand customers, typically factories or premises connected at medium or high voltage, are billed under Special Load Tariff (SLT) categories rather than the standard non-residential band. For example, SLT-LV customers pay 240.2104 GHp/kWh, and SLT-HV customers pay 188.4762 GHp/kWh, each with a service charge of GHS 500 per month, effective 1st July 2026.

cases.query: How does billing work for a customer with rooftop solar under net metering?
cases.reference_answer: A net metering customer with rooftop solar pays the Import Tariff for power drawn from ECG's grid and receives a credit at a lower Export Tariff for surplus power sent back to the grid. For example, in the 31-300 kWh band, the Import Tariff is 122.2505 GHp/kWh and the Export Tariff is 81.5004 GHp/kWh, effective 1st July 2026. The Export Tariff is intentionally set lower than the Import Tariff.

cases.query: Why do ECG's electricity tariffs change so often?
cases.reference_answer: Electricity tariffs in Ghana are set and approved by PURC, not ECG. Besides periodic full Major Tariff Reviews, PURC applies a quarterly Automatic Adjustment (Indexation) Formula that revises tariffs to reflect changes in exchange rates, inflation, and fuel costs. Each new quarterly publication explicitly revokes and replaces the previous gazette, which is why customers should confirm the current rate for their billing period via ECG or purc.com.gh rather than relying on an undated figure.
cases.candidate_answer: ECG's electricity tariffs are approved by PURC and change due to periodic Major Tariff Reviews and routine Automatic Adjustments, which reflect changes in exchange rates, inflation, and fuel costs. Tariffs are typically revised every quarter. For the most current rates, please check the PURC or ECG website.

cases.query: If ECG doesn't resolve my billing complaint, what can I do?
cases.reference_answer: If a billing dispute or service complaint is not resolved by ECG at the District level, you can escalate it to PURC, which has the statutory power to investigate and settle disputes between customers and utility companies. Complaints can be submitted through purc.com.gh or by calling PURC's Accra office on 0302 218 300.
